title: Prices on a minimum-spend floor

blocks.text: A regulator requires a power utility to spend at least a floor $`F_y`$ on vegetation work in each year $`y`$. The utility's plan maximizes value, and the floor rows are the rows that tie its projects together:

\max \; \sum_i \sum_t v_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad
\text{veg}_y(x) \ge F_y \quad \forall y \quad \text{(floor}_y), \qquad \text{and rows on single projects}
To bound the best plan, the planners relax the floor rows with prices $`\mu_y \ge 0`$. Note the direction: these rows are $`\ge`$, not $`\le`$ like the budget rows of the lesson.

Write it first: $`L(\mu)`$ with the floors priced so that every $`\mu \ge 0`$ gives an upper bound, the subgradient of $`L`$ at $`\mu`$ in terms of the relaxed plan's vegetation spend, and the projected update with Polyak's step $`s = \theta\,(L(\mu) - \underline{z}) / \lVert g \rVert^2`$, where $`\underline{z}`$ is the best plan's value so far.

Then write `next_prices(prices, floors, veg_spend, bound, best_value, theta)` to return the next prices as a new dict by year. `veg_spend` is the relaxed plan's vegetation spend by year, `bound` is $`L(\mu)`$ at `prices`. If the subgradient is zero, the relaxed plan meets every floor exactly and the prices are returned unchanged.

cases.says: when the bound equals the best plan's value, the step is zero and the prices do not move
a year whose relaxed plan spends less than its floor gets a higher price, and one above it a lower price
a price that the step would push below zero stops at zero
the step length divides the bound's excess by the sum of the squared subgradient entries
a relaxed plan that spends every floor exactly has a zero subgradient, and the prices stay as they are

origin.section: Subgradient Steps Raise the Price of an Overspent Year and Lower the Price of an Underspent One

concepts: a projected subgradient step with Polyak's step length moves each price by the relaxed plan's unspent or overspent amount
